mercy_translation.text:
When human beings had thus become irrational, and demonic error had so overshadowed everything everywhere and hidden the knowledge of the true God, what was God to do? Was he to remain silent before so great a disaster and allow human beings to be deceived by demons and not to know God?

What need, then, would there have been for the human being to be made according to God's image in the beginning? He should either have been made simply irrational, or, having been made rational, he should not have lived the life of irrational creatures.

What need was there for him to receive a conception of God at the beginning? If he is not worthy to receive it now, it should not have been given to him at the beginning either.

And what benefit would there be to God who made them, or what glory would he have, if the human beings made by him did not worship him but supposed that others had made them? In that case God would be found to have created them for others and not for himself.

Even a human king does not leave the lands he has founded exposed to serve others or flee to others. He reminds them by letters, and often sends messages through friends; and if necessary, he comes himself, putting them to shame by his presence, simply so that they may not serve others and his work become useless.

How much more, then, will God spare his own creatures so that they are not led away from him and become servants of things that do not exist—especially since such error becomes for them a cause of destruction and ruin, and those who once shared in the image of God ought not to perish?

What, then, was God to do? What else had to happen except that what was according to the image should be renewed, so that through it human beings might again be able to know him? And how could this have happened unless the very Image of God, our Savior Jesus Christ, had come? It could not be done through human beings, for they themselves were made according to the image; nor through angels, for they are not themselves the Image. Therefore the Word of God came in his own person so that, as the Image of the Father, he might restore the human being made according to the image.

Yet this again could not have happened unless death and corruption were destroyed.

Therefore he fittingly took a mortal body, so that death might finally be destroyed in it and human beings made according to the image might be renewed. For this need no one else was sufficient except the Image of the Father.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius' distinction between Christ as the Image and human beings as made 'according to the image' is central here.
The restoration of the image and the destruction of death are presented as inseparable aspects of the Incarnation.
